headline: Seabirds and Native Trees Are Saving Islands from Rising Seas
meta_description: New study reveals how seabird guano and native vegetation help atoll islands keep pace with sea-level rise through natural island-building processes.
summary_short: Seabirds and native forests boost island resilience to climate change. Research on 28 atoll islands shows these ecosystems can keep pace with projected sea-level rise.
body:
A new study offers unexpected hope for low-lying atoll islands facing the threat of rising seas: when thriving seabird populations roost in native forests, these islands may actually keep pace with ocean levels through the end of the century. Researchers analyzed ecological data from 28 atoll islands across the Indian and Pacific oceans—including sites in the Seychelles, Chagos Archipelago, and French Polynesia—and discovered that nutrient-rich seabird guano, combined with native vegetation, supercharges the natural processes that build and maintain islands. On rat-free islands with abundant seabirds, reef growth could match the rate of sea-level rise projected under 2 degrees Celsius of warming until 2100. The findings reveal that atoll islands are not passive victims of climate change, but dynamic systems that can be restored to greater resilience.

The story begins with a simple observation. Researchers noticed stark contrasts between islands in the Chagos Archipelago: some were quiet havens of rustling palms, while others teemed with seabirds and the pungent smell of guano. The difference came down to rats. Historical introduction of rats by sailors had eliminated seabirds from many islands, silencing what were once thriving ecosystems. Where seabirds persisted, nutrient-dense guano flowed into the soil and marine waters, triggering cascading benefits: native vegetation grew stronger, fish became more abundant and healthier, and crucially, the reef structures that form the islands' foundation grew faster and recovered more robustly.

The findings point to a practical solution: rewilding atoll islands by removing invasive predators and replanting native forests. This approach offers what researchers call a "win-win-win" outcome—building climate resilience for islands while simultaneously restoring biodiversity and supporting ocean recovery. Rather than portraying atoll communities as helpless against climate change, this research illuminates nature-based solutions already within reach.
quick_facts: Study analyzed 28 atoll islands in Indian and Pacific oceans
Seabird guano boosts reef growth and island resilience
Rat-free islands with seabirds can keep pace with sea-level rise until 2100
Native vegetation binds sediment and prevents coastal erosion
Rewilding offers climate, biodiversity, and ocean recovery benefits
